newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police break fresh protest over savings.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police break fresh protest over savings.

text.p: Around 5,000 Albanians, fearing the loss of their savings in collapsing pyramid schemes, hurled stones at a town hall in the southern town of Lushnje on Friday but police quickly dispersed the crowd, residents said.

Residents in Lushnje, 85 km (55 miles) southwest of Tirana, contacted by telephone, said the crowd gathered in the centre of the town and blocked traffic on the main road from the capital before the protest was halted.
There was one unconfirmed report that police shot in the air but it could not be independently corroborated.
"God help us! All Lushnje has put their money into the Xhaferri and Gjallica (investment schemes). How can we let them gobble up our money?" one woman told Reuters.
Residents said there had been no violence at the demonstration.
"This morning a number of people gathered in the town centre and more joined them every minute. They shouted slogans against the government," one man called Shelqim said.
The Interior Ministry said it would make a statement later on Friday.

The Lushnje protest was the latest bout of popular unrest in two weeks of demonstrations against the crumbling pyramid schemes in which thousands of Albanians across the country have poured their life savings.

Unaccustomed to the ways of a free market, many Albanians living in the former communist country have sold their homes, farms and belongings in the hope of making huge profits after being lured by scheme operators promising returns of around 200 percent.

President Sali Berisha's right-wing government, attempting to quell the wave of protests, on Thursday banned pyramid schemes and warned operators they could face 20-year jail terms if convicted of running disreputable investment funds.

Authorities have already seized around 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited by two collapsed schemes in state-owned banks but the figure may not be enough to quell the anger of Albanians who face ruin.

The Democratic Party government would face a huge struggle to compensate all investors at a time when Europe's poorest nation is facing a budget deficit amounting to around 11 percent of gross domestic product.
Parliament on Thursday deferred consideration of a second draft law concerning compensation for the thousands of investors to a special session on Monday.
Most residents in Lushnje, a poor agricultural area, deposited their cash in at least two schemes -- Xhaferri, and Populli -- whose funds have been frozen.
The managers of both schemes have been detained, Albanian television reported.
Albania's main opposition Socialist Party, viewing the financial crisis as an opportunity to stir political change, on Friday repeated a call on the government to resign.
The Socialists, and other opposition parties, boycotted a general election last May after accusing the Democrats of rigging the vote.
